did_you_know.text: The Bible distinguishes between rain, which falls mainly in the rainy season, and dew, which gathers at night. Both images suggest that wisdom, too, can nourish people gradually.
The phrase “Ascribe greatness” does not mean making God greater; it invites listeners to recognize His greatness and praise Him together.
Before history was preserved in books, family memory and traditions passed down by parents and elders were major ways of preserving the past.
The “apple of the eye” is the pupil, the dark opening at the center of the eye. In biblical Hebrew, it became an image for something precious and delicate that needs protection.
In the ancient Near East, the eagle was a symbol of strength and height. The image of its wings emphasizes protection, carrying, and gradually teaching the young to fly.
“Flint” is an especially hard kind of rock, often associated with sharp stone. Honey in rocky crevices is an image of abundance appearing even in a place that looks barren.
Bashan, mentioned in the verse, was a fertile region east of the Jordan known for its land and fine cattle. “The produce of Bashan” therefore became a biblical symbol of wealth and abundance.
“Jeshurun” is a poetic name for Israel, probably related to the word “upright.” The name meaning “upright” appears here in a criticism of behavior that is not upright.
The word “shedim” is rare in the Bible, appearing only here and in Psalm 106:37. It refers to supernatural beings whose worship is not worship of God.
The verse plays on the phrases “not a people” and “a foolish nation”: a people that angers God with idols is portrayed as losing both its identity and its wisdom.
The word “end” can mean not only a final moment but also the future result of one’s actions. The verse reminds us that wisdom includes thinking about consequences.
Sodom and Gomorrah became biblical symbols of destruction and wickedness. Their vine is therefore pictured as producing bitter and poisonous fruit.
The verse is built from pairs of opposites: killing and giving life, wounding and healing. This poetic structure emphasizes complete power over every extreme.
Hoshea son of Nun is Joshua, the leader who would bring Israel into the land. His original name was Hoshea, and Moses added the letter yod to it.
The phrase “set your hearts” shows that in biblical Hebrew the heart is not only the seat of emotion, but also of thought, will, and understanding.
The Torah is described here as “not an empty word,” meaning it is not pointless or without substance. This reflects the idea that learning and practice can shape life itself.
Mount Nebo lies in the land of Moab, east of the Dead Sea. It belongs to a mountain ridge from which one can look west toward the Jordan region and the land of Canaan.
